new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word; contrastive vowel length is likewise restricted to the initial syllable. Verb roots are relatively unstressed and are treated as forming one phonological word with whatever precedes them, so they do not receive their own initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said by Black 1980. (Goedemans 1998 App. D files Kurtjar under 'initial main stress, secondary on alternates', second-hand from Black's 1977 Ms dictionary.)
new_statements.exceptions: Verb roots are 'relatively unstressed' and show no length contrasts -- Black flags that treating them as part of the preceding word may be 'simplistic'. No lexical exceptions given. Note the sister language Kuthant differs: stress on the first long vowel, else the first vowel (p.197).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word as Black phonologises it (verb root plus preceding material = one word). Statement is the fieldworker's own synchronic analysis ('here taken to'), embedded in a historical-comparative paper; based exclusively on Black's fieldwork from 1974 (p.188). Kurtjar is an initial-dropping language with initial consonant clusters, so 'first syllable' refers to the synchronic (post-loss) word.
new_statements.identity_note: Black 1980 describes Kurtjar proper (self-name kurtYar, also elicited as 'Kunggara'), including Rib/Areba as an indistinguishable dialect; data 'dialectally homogeneous' and exclusively from Black's own fieldwork from 1974. Same section gives a separate, different statement for the sister language Kuthant (kuth1240: stress on first long vowel, else first vowel) -- do not conflate.

sources.note: The work never mentions Kurtjar (nor Gunggara/Kuthant/Norman Pama), so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's fixed: initial syllable record; its Australia-wide generalisation (initial main stress is the majority pattern) is merely compatible with it. The citation's parenthetical '(Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map)' refers to Figure 1 on p. 66, an Arnhem Land map on which Miriwung is number 51; it has nothing to do with Kurtjar and looks like a note carried over from another language's record.
